summary: Councilors approved a joint press release on the Medford High School project, with a public comment process added to joint meetings. They tabled a $269,295.81 Law Department budget request until November 17, 2026, and sent a Fire Department drone use policy to committee. They also asked the administration for an update on a possible sale of Cataldo Ambulance Service.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE – November X, 2026 
Contact: Steve Smirti and Will Pipicelli 
 
Medford’s Elected Officials Support the Medford High School Building Project and 
Outline Next Steps for Cost Estimates  
Estimated tax impacts will be released based on accurate final cost estimates in February after 
completion of Schematic Design process 
  
(MEDFORD) — Medford’s elected officials in the Mayor’s Office, City Council, and School 
Committee support the Medford Comprehensive High School Building Project. The city will 
release the final tax impact estimate for the debt exclusion in February, once Schematic Design 
is complete and the city’s chosen construction manager, Suffolk Construction, has developed 
accurate final cost estimates. 
 
The Medford Comprehensive High School Building Committee approved the Project Scope and 
Space Summary on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, which advances the project to the Schematic 
Design phase of the MSBA (Massachusetts School Building Authority) process.  
 
Why do we need a new Medford High School? 
• The Medford High School building is more than 50 years old and is 
deteriorating, with failing systems that frequently disrupt student learning and create 
significant stress for students, parents, and staff.   
o Plumbing issues have forced the school to close several weeks ago, causing 
stress and hassle for students, teachers, and parents.   
o Ongoing and recurring issues include burst heating pipes that force sections of 
the school to close temporarily; insufficient insulation and HVAC systems that 
require students to wear winter hats, gloves, and coats in their classrooms while 
trying to learn; and a leaking roof that requires continuous maintenance even 
during school hours. 
• Vocational and special education programming require more space.  
o More than half of MHS students are enrolled in vocational programming, and 
annually 6-7 programs have a wait list.
7 
 
o Special education spaces constrain how we support specialized learning needs. 
o State educational safety standards require larger, updated facilities to meet the 
significant demand from our Medford students. 
• The cost to renovate in Medford may end up higher than the cost to rebuild.  
o The MHS Building Committee, architect, and project manager investigated more 
than 29 options for renovating the current building.  
o Renovating and upgrading the existing High School Building to current building 
codes, simply “fixing” what exists today and meeting modern safety, building 
code, and accessibility standards, would cost approximately $478 million.  
o The City would pay the entire cost, without any MSBA state fund reimbursement, 
because a code-update project would not meet our educational needs, such as 
expanded vocational and special education programming. Any significant 
investment in repairs to the building would make a full code upgrade legally 
required. 
 
What will the cost impact be to Medford residents? 
 
• The City is proposing a debt exclusion for voter approval to pay for this project by 
repaying construction bonds over 30 years.  
• Based on the most recent estimate for the selected design for the new High School, the 
total project cost is estimated to be just below $700 million, with the State paying an 
estimated $226 million and the City paying an estimated $474 million.  
• The project team will continue looking for design efficiencies during the design phase, 
selecting cost-effective materials, and carefully evaluating phasing options so the 
community rallies behind this much-needed project. 
• Final construction cost estimates, the city’s share of this project, and the cost impact of 
the debt exclusion on taxpayers will be available in early February 2027. 
• While the MHS Building Committee has already reduced the project's total cost by over 
$150 million since March, the City can also mitigate cost impacts in multiple ways, 
including allocating new property tax growth from new development projects, reserving 
resources now to pay for debt service later, and maximizing all local property tax 
exemptions available to residents under state law. 
• Medford Public Schools staff and MHS project team members have also applied for 
other state, federal, and private grants and started private fundraising efforts to help fund 
portions of the project. 
• Please visit the MHS Project page (www.medfordhsproject.com) to learn more about the 
design process, the significant impacts of cost escalations on high school construction 
projects, and the existing programs at MHS that must be incorporated into the new 
building.

26-200 - Resolution Inquiring Into the Contractual and Community Impacts of the Sale of 
Cataldo Ambulance Service 
Offered by George Scarpelli, City Councilor, Anna Callahan, City Councilor, Isaac Bears, 
Council President 
 
Whereas, emergency medical services and reliable ambulance transport are critical 
components of public safety, health, and welfare for the residents of our community; and 
 
Whereas, Cataldo Ambulance Service currently serves as the primary provider of emergency 
medical and transport services under negotiated agreements with the city; and 
 
Whereas, reports and discussions have emerged regarding a potential sale of Cataldo 
Ambulance Service; and 
 
Whereas, any transition in ownership, management, or corporate structure of a primary 
emergency services vendor introduces potential uncertainties regarding service continuity, 
response times, staffing levels, and the enforcement of existing public agreements; and 
 
Whereas, the City Council seeks to proactively protect the public interest, ensure strict 
adherence to previously negotiated terms, and understand any legal or operational 
contingencies available to the municipality; now, therefore: 
 
Be it Resolved by the Medford City Council that we respectfully request that the City 
Administration, including the Mayor's Office, and relevant public safety officials, to provide a 
formal update and comprehensive analysis regarding the potential sale of Cataldo Ambulance 
Service; and 
 
Be it Further Resolved that this inquiry specifically requests the Administration to clarify: 
1. The exact legal and contractual impacts a sale would have on the community and the 
active agreements currently in place. 
2. Whether existing contracts contain assignability clauses, performance guarantees, or 
change-of-control provisions that protect the city's interests. 
3. What measures the Administration is taking to guarantee that emergency medical 
service levels, response times, and local staffing remain uncompromised. 
 
Be it Further Resolved that the City Council receive an update on businesses that have 
complained that Cataldo Ambulance is using their private parking lots as bases of operations 
due to the continued lack of a fixed base of operation for Cataldo in the City of Medford. 
 
Be it Finally Resolved that the Administration be requested to provide a written response or 
appear before the City Council at it’s next regularly scheduled meeting to brief the body on 
these matters.

PURPOSE 
The Purpose of this procedure is to provide members of the Medford Fire Department 
(MFD) with a set of operational guidelines intended to promote safe, efficient, and lawful 
operation of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS). This document identifies the 
responsibilities, requirements, and operations of the Department’s UAS program.  
The MFD’s primary purpose for integrating UAS technology into its initial hazard-mitigation 
deployment model is to increase the Incident Commander’s (IC) “situational awareness” 
by providing a unique aerial perspective that assists the IC in fully understanding the 
challenges of a given incident in “real time”; thus, providing critical information necessary 
to guide decision-making. Ultimately, those decisions impact the risk posed to firefighters 
and equipment.  
 
POLICY 
It shall be the policy of the Medford Fire Department to use UAS to enhance the 
Department’s mission of protecting lives and property. Any use of UAS will be in strict 
accordance with federal, state, and local laws, including compliance with Constitutional 
and Privacy Rights, and FAA regulations.  
 
DEFINITIONS AND ABBREVIATIONS 
Above Ground Level (AGL): AGL is the altitude expressed in the actual number of feet 
measured above the ground.  
Air Traffic Control (ATC): Manages traffic from the airport to a radius of 3 to 30 miles. 
Provides pilots taxiing and take-off instructions, air traffic clearance, and advice based on 
their own observations and experience. Maintains separations between landing and 
departing aircraft, transfers control of aircraft to the enroute center controllers when the 
aircraft leave their airspace and receives control of aircraft on flights entering their 
airspace.

Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS): The operation of UAS at distances outside the visual 
line of sight (VLOS), as defined herein.  
Certificate of Authorization (COA): Issued by the FAA and grants permission to fly within 
specific boundaries and parameters.  
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA): Federal agency in the United States and part of the 
Department of Transportation (DOT). The FAA regulates US civil aviation, US commercial 
space transportation, operates control towers, builds, installs, and maintains electronic 
aids to navigation, and registers all pilots and aircraft in the United States.  
National Airspace System (NAS): The NAS is made up of a network of air navigation 
facilities, ATC facilities, airports, technology, and appropriate rules and regulations that are 
needed to operate the system.  
Navigable Airspace: FAA-controlled airspace classified as: A, B, C, D, E, and G.  
Notice to Airmen (NOTAM): A NOTAM is time-critical information concerning the 
establishment, condition, or change in any component in the NAS. The NOTAM provides 
knowledge that is essential to personnel concerned with flight operations in designated 
areas. NOTAMs may be filed as a temporary change to the NAS as they were not known in 
advance to publish on aeronautical charts or other operational publications.  
Personal Identifying Information: For purposes of this policy, this includes a person’s 
date of birth, social-security number, personal telephone number, home address, personal 
email address, official state or government-issued driver’s license or identification number.  
Remote Pilot-in-Command (RPIC): Person who has final authority and responsibility for 
the operation and safety of flight, has been designated as the RPIC before or during the 
flight, and holds the appropriate category, class, and type rating, if applicable, for the 
conduct of the flight. Pilots are authorized to evaluate and accept or decline any mission or 
portion thereof due to safety concerns.  
Person Manipulating the Controls: A person who is manipulating the UAS flight controls. 
The RPIC must be able to take control of the UAV from the person manipulating the 
controls in case of an emergency. This can be done by standing close enough to physically

take the controller, by using a secondary controller, or use of a pre-programmed safe-mode 
system.  
Unmanned Aircraft Vehicle (UAV): A powered, aerial vehicle that uses aerodynamic forces 
to provide vehicle lift, can fly autonomously or be piloted remotely, and can be expendable 
or recoverable. Refers more specifically to the unmanned aircraft itself.  
Unmanned Aircraft System (UAS): Consists of an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 
55 lbs., the command system, a secure control link, camera, and other related safety 
support equipment, including ground control base stations and specialty vehicles 
designated to support unmanned flight operations. 
Unmanned Aircraft System Crewmember: A Pilot in Command, Visual Observer, or other 
persons assigned UAS duties for the purpose of the flight.  
Visual Line of Sight (VLOS): Visual contact between RPIC or VO and a UAS sufficient to 
maintain safe operational control of the aircraft, known location, and be able to scan the 
airspace in which it is operating to see and avoid other aircraft or objects aloft or on the 
ground. Under the current VLOS COA the RPIC and person manipulating the controls must 
retain the capability to see the aircraft unaided except for corrective lenses 
Visual Observer (VO): the VO is for the visual observation of the UAV while in flight. The VO 
shall alert the PIC of any conditions (obstructions, terrain, structures, air traffic, weather, 
etc.) that may affect the safety of flight.  
 
SCOPE 
The purpose of this SOP is to provide the process and procedures for the operations and 
management of any small UAS used by the MFD. It will detail the conditions under which 
the MFD will utilize UAS technology to maximize efficiency and cost savings while 
minimizing the risk to first responders, equipment, and the community.  
UAS program development is focused on strategic and tactical support of emergency 
service delivery, planned events, investigations, and training.

LEGAL AUTHORITY 
4th Amendment Protections, Privacy and Civil Liberties 
It is the policy of the Medford Fire Department that the operation of UAS shall be carried out 
in a manner that respects and protects personal privacy consistent with the United States 
Constitution and Federal, State, and local laws. The impact on privacy and civil liberties 
shall be balanced against the governmental interests leading to deployment. As such, the 
Medford Fire Department shall not retain any photographs or video recordings of any 
incidents or training missions. If any photographs or video recordings are taken in error, the 
UAS Program Coordinator will be notified at the conclusion of the operation, and the 
photographs or video recordings will be deleted.  
The Medford Fire Department will use the Department of Homeland Security “Best 
Practices for Protecting Privacy, Civil Rights & Civil Liberties in Unmanned Aircraft Systems 
Programs” (12/18/2015) as its framework for protection of applicable rights to individuals.  
The Medford Fire Department prohibits the collection, use, retention, or dissemination of 
UAS live footage that would: 
a. Be used or operated to violate a person’s reasonable expectation of privacy, if a 
warrant has not been obtained, there is no exigency, and/or there is no consent. 
Some factors to include that may create a reasonable expectation of privacy are: (1) 
the location is not open to public use; (2) the location is privately owned and the 
person on the property has the right to control access to the location and exclude 
others; and (3) the location is one where the owner has taken normal precautions to 
maintain privacy. A person does not have a reasonable expectation of privacy in

Structure Fires – Deployment of UAS to structure fires, in particular, buildings suspected of 
structural compromise, i.e. roof, walls, or other components. UAS will be utilized during the 
initial action phase as well as the extinguishment and overhaul phase of an incident.  
Rescue Operations – Deployment of UAS into wildland/woodland areas to verify the 
existence and location of lost or injured persons and confirm the safest and most effective 
means of dispatching Department rescue teams to make patient contact and extract them 
from the area.

camera capabilities to assist in identifying potential hazardous-materials indicators, 
affected areas, thermal anomalies, and observable conditions.

BEYOND VISUAL LINE OF SIGHT (BVLOS) OPERATIONS 
PURPOSE AND AUTHORITY 
This SOP governs Medford Fire Department (MFD) small UAS flights under FAA Certificate 
of Waiver (COW) 91.113-2026-01101, including BVLOS flights without a visual observer 
(VO). Operations must qualify as Public Aircraft Operations and comply with the waiver, its 
application, and any associated COA or airspace authorization. Where requirements 
conflict, follow the most restrictive unless the FAA authorizes otherwise. The COW does 
not authorize prohibited or restricted airspace. [COW pp. 1–3; SP 1–9] 
MFD is responsible to the FAA for safe operations; the RPIC is responsible for flight safety. 
Incident objectives do not supersede aviation limitations. [SP 1, 3, 22–24] 
PERSONNEL, TRAINING, AND DOCUMENTS 
Personnel. Use only RPICs trained and certified by MFD. Ensure RPICs, control 
manipulators, and VOs (if assigned) are familiar with the waiver and Part 91. Document 
training, including night-vision physiology and visual-illusion training for RPICs/VOs. [SP 1, 
13] 
Records. Keep current pilot-name and aircraft-registration lists, and an accessible copy of 
this COW at the ground control station. An RPIC or VO may not serve more than one UA at a 
time unless authorized. [SP 4–6, 16] 
AUTHORIZED FLIGHT ENVELOPE 
BVLOS altitude. Class G: at/below 200 ft AGL, OR up to 100 ft above an obstruction within a 
100-ft radius of the UA (maximum 400 ft AGL). Class B/C/D/E surface areas: at/below 200 ft 
AGL and within the applicable UAS Facility Map (UASFM) height, whichever is lower. [SP 11]

SEPARATION ASSURANCE STANDARDS 
All UAS operations shall remain within the altitude limitations established by the applicable 
FAA Certificate of Authorization, waiver, or other approved operating authority. For Class B 
airspace, the RPIC shall verify the current UAS Facility Map altitude before flight. BVLOS 
operations shall comply with the additional altitude restrictions specified in FAA Waiver 
91.113-2026-01101. The general 400-foot AGL limitation shall not be interpreted as 
authorization to exceed any more restrictive approved altitude. 
UAS shall give right-of-way to manned aircraft and return to its landing area until flight 
becomes safe again.  
If multiple UAS are operating in a single operational area, the RPICs of each aircraft must 
communicate and at a minimum, maintain 20 feet separation in all directions. 20 feet 
separation alone does not guarantee safe separation. An approved deconfliction plan 
based on aircraft speed, positioning accuracy, mission area, and contingencies is required. 
 
LOST LINK/GNSS PROCEDURES 
Lost link is an interruption or loss of the Command and Control (C2) link between the 
control station and the unmanned aircraft. This prevents control of the aircraft and results 
in the aircraft performing its pre-set lost-link procedure. 
While operating in controlled airspace, in the event of a lost link, the RPIC, or another 
designated crew member when available, shall notify the appropriate ATC facility as 
required by the applicable COA. 
The following lost-link and GNSS/GPS procedures shall apply: 
• Prior to flight, the RPIC shall verify that the aircraft Signal Lost behavior is 
configured to Return to Home (RTH) and that the home point and RTH altitude are 
appropriate for the operating area and comply with applicable airspace and altitude 
limitations.

• Upon loss of the C2 link, the aircraft will attempt to re-establish the connection. If 
the C2 link is not re-established within 3 seconds, the aircraft will execute the 
preset Signal Lost behavior. When configured for RTH, the aircraft will return to the

• The nature of the emergency 
• Aircraft altitude, last known location, and direction of flight 
• Remaining battery/flight time 
• RPIC intentions 
• Termination or status of the emergency condition

UAS SPECIFICATIONS 
Global Positioning System – All MFD UAS will have a global positioning system,  
Obstacle Avoidance – All MFD UAS will be equipped with obstacle avoidance.  
Remote ID – All MFD UAS will have RID embedded or RID broadcast modules.  
Software/Firmware Updates – MFD will ensure the software and/or firmware used to 
operate each UAS is kept up to date and maintained. The Program Coordinator will be 
responsible for overseeing this. The UAS Team will confirm that updates are current prior to 
each use. The UAS will not operate until the software update has been completed.  
Aircraft Features – No MFD UAS may be modified or be used in a way that would be 
reasonable considered to distract drivers or other aircraft.  
Airworthiness – The RPIC will be responsible for ensuring the UAS is flight-ready according 
to manufacturer recommendations and any related industry standards. A pre-flight 
checklist will be utilized prior to ALL UAS flights.  
Strobe – All MFD UAS must have a strobe light that meets FAA night visibility regulations 
and an adequate flash rate that is visible for 3 statute miles. The strobe will remain on 
during all flight operations, day or night.

• The serial number, make, and model of each MFD UAS. 
• The secured location where each MFD UAS is stored. 
• A description of the technologies and capabilities associated with each UAS. 
• Dates upon which new updates to the UAS or associated technology are required.  
• Track UAS lifespan and replacement.

includes efforts to protect the UAS from cyber tampering or attack.

D/NOTAM FILING PROCEDURES

1. Obtain GPS coordinates prior to calling. 
2. Call 1-877-487-6867 
3. Enter 22

Requests to Operate Outside the Approved Operating Area (Mutual Aid) 
 
1. Obtain GPS coordinates prior to calling.  
2. Call System Operations Support Center (SOSC) at 202-267-8276. 
3. Provide the following information: 
a. Name and contact number 
b. Confirm you are operating under an active COA. (COA number is 2026-ESA-
19370-COA, expires October 15, 2028) 
c. Mission title (structure fire, search, etc.) 
d. Date, time, and duration of the flight(s) 
e. Mission area boundaries 
f. Aircraft make, model, and registration (Autel Evo Max 4T XE, Registration # 
FA3ELPFERF expires June 12, 2029) 
g. Flight altitude requested 
h. Nature of the operation – firefighting, wildfire suppression, search and 
rescue, damage assessment, disaster recovery) 
i. Indicate why standard COA/107 processes cannot be used (time-sensitive, 
airspace restrictions, emergency situation) 
4. Call SOSC when mission is completed to cancel the request.
